notes.b: Food starts to spoil as soon as it is harvested or slaughtered. Preservation means treating food so that spoilage is slowed or stopped and the food can be kept, moved and eaten later, with colour, flavour, texture and nutritive value as near as possible to fresh.
points: It reduces waste by keeping surplus produce, such as a glut of home-grown fruit or vegetables, usable for months rather than days, instead of being thrown away.
Because less food is thrown away, preservation also reduces the environmental footprint of food.
It makes food available out of season and over long distances, so perishable foods (those that spoil quickly) can be transported and stored.
It makes food safer by destroying food poisoning micro-organisms or stopping them from growing, and it lengthens shelf life (the time food stays good to eat).
It creates foods with distinct textures and flavours, such as jam, chutney, dried fruit, smoked fish and cured meat, which increases variety and choice.
notes.tip: If asked to discuss two advantages, name each one and then develop it in a sentence or two: say what it means for the household or the industry, not just the name.

notes.b: Spoilage is not caused only by micro-organisms. Several separate processes make food unusable, and each has its own visible effect.
points: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions and are naturally present in food. After harvest or slaughter they carry on working, so food ripens, softens, darkens and changes flavour even when no micro-organism is present. Cut apple, banana and potato brown this way.

Micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) grow on food, causing decay, rot, souring, off-odours and slime, and in some cases food poisoning. Moulds give fuzzy growth on bread, cheese and jam; yeasts ferment fruit juice and jam, with bubbling and an alcoholic smell; bacteria cause souring, putrefaction and food poisoning.
Putrefaction is the breakdown of proteins by bacteria, producing foul-smelling products.

Oxidation occurs when oxygen reacts with fats, causing rancidity (an unpleasant, stale taste and smell), and with the cut surfaces of fruit and vegetables, causing browning. Vitamin C is also lost by oxidation.
Moisture loss through the skins of fruit and vegetables causes shrivelling, wilting, wrinkling and loss of weight. It also dries and hardens bread and cheese.
Incorrect storage temperature allows micro-organisms and enzymes to work quickly, because warmth speeds both of them up.
Poor hygiene and careless handling carry micro-organisms from unwashed hands, equipment, pests or raw food onto prepared food.

Chemical contaminants, such as insecticide or pesticide residues, antibiotics, metals and residues from cleaning products, can make food unsafe. Physical damage such as bruising also opens food to spoilage.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for three or four distinct causes, so make each cause its own point and give its visible effect. Do not write only about micro-organisms: enzymes, oxidation and moisture loss act with no organisms present.

notes.b: Micro-organisms need six conditions to grow and multiply. Every preservation method works by removing or controlling one or more of them.
points: The six conditions are food (nutrients), moisture (available water), warmth (a suitable temperature), time (to multiply), a suitable pH or acidity and, for aerobic ones (those that need air), oxygen. Most bacteria prefer a neutral or slightly acid pH.

Bacteria that cause food poisoning multiply rapidly in the danger zone of 5 to 63 °C, which is why chilled and hot food is kept outside it. Below 5 °C growth is slowed; above 63 °C it is stopped and most are killed by sustained heat.
Under good conditions one bacterial cell divides about every 20 minutes (binary fission, splitting in two), so numbers rise very fast.
Moulds and yeasts tolerate acid, sugar and low moisture better than most bacteria, so they spoil jam and dried fruit.
Moulds appear as fuzzy colonies or threads; yeasts produce bubbling, gas and a sour or alcoholic smell.
Enzymes work best at a moderate temperature and are destroyed (denatured) by heat or strong acid; cold slows them but does not stop them.
Micro-organisms cannot multiply in food with little available water, which is why drying and concentrated sugar or salt preserve food.
notes.tip: Always link a method to the condition it removes or controls. Marks go to the principle, not to the recipe.

notes.b: Three groups of micro-organism spoil food, and spores and enzymes also have to be understood. Each acts differently, which is why different methods suit different foods.
points: Bacteria are single-celled organisms; some cause food poisoning and others spoil food by producing acid and gas.
Yeasts are single-celled fungi that ferment sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Moulds are multicellular fungi that grow as visible threads and spread by airborne spores.
Spores are dormant (resting), resistant forms produced by some bacteria and all moulds; they survive ordinary heat and cold and start growing again when conditions improve.
Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein, and each one acts on a specific substance in food.

notes.h: Osmosis and its role in preservation
notes.b: Osmosis explains why strong sugar or salt solutions preserve food. It is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane (one that lets water through but not most dissolved substances) from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
points: The cell membrane of a micro-organism is partially permeable, so water leaves the cell when the surrounding solution is concentrated.
Loss of water makes the cell shrink and stop growing, and at high concentrations it can kill the cell.

The same process draws water out of food, which is why salted meat and fish and sugared fruit keep. A strong sugar or salt solution outside a microbial cell draws water out, so the cell shrivels and cannot multiply.
notes.tip: Describe the principle in terms of which condition is removed: here, available water is drawn out of the organisms by osmosis.

notes.h: The principles that underlie every method
notes.b: Every preservation method works by removing or controlling one or more of the conditions that micro-organisms and enzymes need, and by preventing re-contamination. There are only a few principles, and each method is an application of one or more of them.
points: Destroy micro-organisms and inactivate enzymes with heat, as in canning, bottling, jam and chutney making, pasteurisation, sterilisation and blanching. Irradiation also destroys organisms and some enzymes.
Slow or stop activity with low temperature: refrigeration slows growth and enzyme action, and freezing makes organisms dormant (inactivated, not killed) and makes water unavailable as ice.
Remove available water: dehydration (drying, freeze drying) takes water away, while sugar and salt tie it up and draw it out of organisms by osmosis, as in jam, salted fish and cured meat.

Alter the pH with acid: vinegar (acetic acid) in pickles and chutney, or acids produced in fermentation, such as lactic acid in yoghurt and sauerkraut and acetic acid in vinegar. This prevents the growth of many spoilage and food poisoning bacteria.
Use chemical preservatives that inhibit organisms: sugar, salt, vinegar, smoke, alcohol and permitted additives such as sulphur dioxide, sorbates, benzoates and nitrite.

Exclude oxygen and prevent re-entry of organisms with airtight packaging, vacuum sealing, sealed hot jars (a vacuum forms as the contents cool) and moisture-proof wraps for the freezer. Removing oxygen also inactivates enzymes.
Prevent re-contamination after treatment, using sterilised jars and lids, clean utensils, good hygiene and sealing straight away.
Most methods combine principles. Jam uses heat, sugar (osmosis), acid and pectin, and a sealed jar; chutney uses heat, vinegar and sugar; smoked fish uses salt, drying and smoke chemicals.
notes.tip: Freezing and drying only stop organisms growing, and they restart after thawing or rehydration, so say inactivated or dormant, never killed. For a surplus of home-grown fruit or vegetables, name the method and then the principle: which condition is removed or which organism is destroyed. A revision table matching each spoilage cause to the principle and method that controls it helps.

notes.b: The methods of preservation fall into groups according to the principle they use. Knowing the groups shows the structure of food preservation.
points: Low temperature: refrigeration and freezing.
Heat: canning, bottling, jam and chutney making, pasteurisation, sterilisation and blanching.
Water removal: drying and freeze drying, and sugar or salt that bind water.
Chemicals: sugar, salt, vinegar, smoke, alcohol and permitted additives, with sugar, vinegar, salt, smoking and alcohol being the traditional natural preservatives.
Fermentation and irradiation.
notes.tip: Be ready to name three methods of preservation with an example food each, such as heat, freezing and a chemical method, with fruit, vegetables, meat or fish as the foods. Sugar and vinegar are the usual answer for two natural preservatives; salt, smoking and alcohol are also accepted.

keyTerms.definition: Any change in food, caused by enzymes, micro-organisms, oxidation or moisture loss, that makes it unpleasant or unsafe to eat.
A living organism too small to see without a microscope, such as a bacterium, yeast or mould.
A protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction in food, such as ripening or browning, without being used up.
The movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one.
A reaction between food and oxygen that causes rancidity in fats and browning on cut surfaces.
A dormant, heat-resistant form produced by some bacteria and moulds that survives unfavourable conditions.
The temperature range of 5 to 63 °C in which food poisoning bacteria multiply rapidly.
Any treatment that stops or slows the spoilage of food so that it can be stored safely for longer.

factCards.definition: Reducing waste, making food available out of season, making food safer, and enabling perishable food to be transported and stored.
Enzyme action, microbial contamination and moisture loss through the skin.
Food, acidity, temperature, time, oxygen and moisture.

questions.prompt: Explain how enzymes cause food to spoil, and name one way the action of enzymes can be controlled.
questions.model: Enzymes are natural proteins present in food that continue to ripen, soften, darken and change flavour after harvest or slaughter. They act on specific substances in the food, so the food changes even when no micro-organisms are present. Control: blanching destroys enzymes with heat; cold storage slows enzyme action; acids such as lemon juice inactivate enzymes.

questions.prompt: Discuss the principles of food preservation, explaining how the causes of spoilage are controlled by each principle.
questions.model: Causes of spoilage: enzymes, micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds), oxidation and moisture loss, and incorrect storage temperature. Principles: destroy or remove micro-organisms by heat, irradiation or chemicals such as salt, sugar and vinegar. Inactivate enzymes by blanching, heat or acid. Prevent re-contamination by clean, airtight packaging. Control available water by dehydration or by binding water with sugar or salt, using osmosis. Control temperature by freezing, which slows growth, or heat processing, which stops it. Control pH by adding acid.
